title: Chocolate Malt Sourdough Waffles
changes_from_base: The batter starts the night before as a wholemeal sourdough sponge, then gets cocoa, malted milk powder, cinnamon and chocolate chips; no buttermilk, and no whipped cream or fruit to serve.
summary: Deep, malty chocolate waffles built on an overnight sourdough sponge, with melted pockets of chocolate running through.
equipment: wire rack set in a rimmed baking tray

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
dark or semi-sweet chocolate chips (mini chips work well)

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: Mix 227 g ripe sourdough starter, 283 ml cool water and 170 g wholemeal flour in a large bowl, cover and leave at room temperature overnight, about 12 h.

steps.title: Warm
steps.text: Heat the oven to 95°C with a wire rack set in a baking tray inside, then heat the waffle iron and brush it lightly with 1 tsp oil.

steps.title: Sift
steps.text: Sift 43 g cocoa, 71 g malted milk powder, 1 tsp baking powder, ¾ tsp fine salt, ½ tsp cinnamon and 149 g caster sugar into a bowl.

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Stir the sifted ingredients into the overnight sponge with 2 eggs, 85 g melted butter, 2 tsp vanilla and 128 g chocolate chips until combined.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Cook the batter in the hot iron following its usual timing until deeply chocolatey and set.

steps.title: Hold
steps.text: Transfer waffles to the rack in the oven, where they will crisp further as they wait.

steps.title: Store
steps.text: Freeze any leftovers for a few weeks and reheat straight from frozen in a toaster.

tips: Start the sponge the night before so the starter has time to ferment and flavour the batter.
Malted milk powder contains barley and milk, so check this suits everyone at the table.
Let waffles rest on the rack in a low oven rather than stacking them, so they stay crisp rather than steaming.
storage: Freeze leftover waffles for a few weeks and reheat them straight from frozen in a toaster. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
